title: Indo-Iranian migrations (contested)
summary: How Indo-Iranian-speaking groups spread across Central Asia is disputed. A 2019 ancient-DNA study found steppe-pastoralist ancestry in outlier individuals at Bronze Age oasis sites such as Gonur by about 2100–1700 BCE, and later in South Asia, and read this as a likely route for Indo-European languages. A 2022 study says links between ancient and modern Indo-Iranian speakers remain unclear.

uncertainty.note: The 2019 study gives steppe ancestry in Turan by 2100 BCE, outliers at BMAC sites about 2100 to 1700 BCE, and integration in South Asia in the first half of the second millennium BCE. Other scholars date the Indo-Iranian spread differently; no such view was read on an opened page.

as_recorded.value: Steppe pastoralist-derived ancestry arrived in Turan by 2100 BCE; BMAC communities regularly interacting with peoples carrying such ancestry by ~2100 to 1700 BCE
Steppe ancestry integrated further south in the first half of the second millennium BCE

when.display: c. 2100–1700 BCE (steppe-related ancestry reaching BMAC sites; later in South Asia)

importance.justification: Bears on the spread of Indo-European languages and the origins of later Iranian and Indo-Aryan peoples.

reviewer_note: Contested. Views on opened pages: (1) Narasimhan et al. 2019 read steppe-derived ancestry in Central and South Asia as a likely conduit for Indo-European languages and found the main BMAC population carried none; (2) Scientific Reports 2022 says the relation between modern Indo-Iranian speakers and ancient southern Central Asian populations remains unclear and shows continuity from the Iron Age. Archaeological disputes (Andronovo versus BMAC) were seen only in search snippets and are not recorded. The pin is a reference site, not an origin.
